description: Mission control here! MISSION ODYSSEY is a Cairo team turning NASA science into a Mars adventure for kids aged 7–12. Young players run a base at Gale Crater, balancing oxygen, water, food and radiation with real numbers from NASA and the Curiosity rover. We love science, education and making learning fun. We need crew members who code (JavaScript/games), design (UI/UX, art) or tell great stories for kids. Ready for launch? Join our crew!
summary:
Mission Odyssey is a browser game that trains children aged 7-12 to think like a real space crew. The child commands Gale Station, a small base for four crew in Gale Crater on Mars, the crater where NASA's Curiosity rover works.

In Mission 01, "The Missing Cargo" (about 8-12 minutes), the child inspects the base's oxygen, water, power and weather, reacts to a real solar radiation alert, drives a rover through a boulder field to a supply lander, and must choose one crate out of five, because the rover can carry only one. The game then runs the base forward one Mars day (sol) at a time and shows what that choice meant: for example, "food runs out on sol 23; resupply arrives on sol 26."

This answers the "Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge by letting children practise what a crew does on a mission: observe, decide under limits, and live with the consequences. The consequences are calculated from NASA numbers: crew oxygen, water and food use from NASA's life-support reference (BVAD), radiation measured by Curiosity, and nine real solar events from NASA's DONKI database, including whether the real forecast came in time. Every number in the game is labelled as NASA measured, NASA forecast, NASA model, NASA reference, Calculated, or Game rule, so children also learn the difference between a measurement and a game rule.

Mission Odyssey teaches children through real decision-making and visible consequences. It supports Arabic and English, two age modes.
details:
Mission Odyssey is a 3D browser game for children aged 7-12. Before playing, the child picks English or Arabic and an age mode: Cadet (7-9, simple words) or Commander (10-12, adds science units). Noor, a friendly robot base assistant, guides the child throughout with voiced lines and subtitles that are always on.

Mission 01, "The Missing Cargo", has 8 phases:

1. Read the briefing.

2. Inspect the base: oxygen, water, power, weather. The greenhouse and antenna are optional stops.

3. Survive a solar particle (radiation) alert.

4. Prepare the rover.

5. Drive about 90 m through a boulder field.

6. Choose ONE of five crates. The rover carries only one.

7. Return to base.

8. Install the crate and send a report, then see the debrief.

Each run hides one of three faults (leaking water recycler, failing battery cells, or broken greenhouse lights) and replays one of nine real NASA solar-event days, giving 27 combinations. The mission can fail if oxygen runs out or CO2 reaches 2.00 kPa, the emergency level quoted in NASA's BVAD, and the game explains why.

MAIN USE: THE CARGO DECISION (input, process, output)

- Input: what the child observed during inspection (for example "Grow lights: LED driver failed"), the resource status, and optionally Mission Control's advice if the child fixed the antenna.

- Process: the child picks one crate. The game runs the same outpost simulation forward, sol by sol, using NASA BVAD crew rates (for example 0.895 kg of oxygen per crew member per day) with every system as the child left it.

- Output: a debrief with a 26-sol outlook (for example "food runs out on sol 23; resupply arrives on sol 26"), the real problem at the base, every decision made, the radiation dose, a score, and "What you learned" cards with NASA sources.

HOW THE DATA SUPPORTS IT

The trade-offs run on NASA's own numbers, so a wrong choice fails for the same reason it would on a real mission.

- Radiation decision: everyone to the shelter (lowest dose, but about 2 hours lost while a dust storm approaches), crew to the shelter while the child works outside (higher personal dose), or everyone keeps working (no time lost, higher dose for all). In our test runs the simulated crew dose was about 64 microgray with the shelter versus about 141 microgray when working. Normal outdoor radiation (6.40 microgray per hour) comes from Curiosity's RAD detector.

- Real forecast timing: with the antenna fixed, the warning time equals the real lead time of that archived DONKI event (first REleASE forecast versus first SOHO detection): +25, -19, +93, -4, -14, +152 and -12 minutes, with no forecast on two days. If the real forecast was late or missing, the child gets no warning, and the game explains why.

- Other trade-offs: charging the rover uses 8 kWh of base power; folding the solar panels protects them from dust but makes less power; switching off grow lights saves power but hurts crops; fixing the antenna brings Mission Control's advice after a 12-minute delay. Causes chain together: dusty panels mean less power, the CO2 scrubber shuts down, and CO2 reaches the danger level within about 6 sols in the outlook.

WORKING FEATURES (verified in play-testing on 14 November)

- Two age modes: Cadet and Commander.

- Kid-friendly status bar: each resource shows a word and a shape (OK / Low / Danger), not colour alone; time left as "N sols left"; units behind a "Units" button; one-time explainer cards for sol, EVA and dose; a kid question above each objective ("Do we have enough air?").

- English and Arabic, with a full right-to-left layout.

- Noor: 77 voice lines, subtitles always on, hints after 45 seconds without progress, 11 verified science facts, mute and volume controls. Audio is built in, with no text-to-speech or internet at run time.

- Cinematic scenes: intro, radiation alert, cargo choice, mission success or failure.

- Data honesty: every number carries a badge (NASA measured / NASA forecast / NASA model / NASA reference / Calculated / Game rule), and a "NASA Science & Data" page lists each dataset, its limits, its validation status and all game assumptions.

- Debrief cards with NASA research: fresh food in space (OSDR OSD-745), crew health (Inspiration4; the card says the game calculates no health effects), and Mars versus ISS radiation (Mars about 0.15-0.31 mGy/day from Curiosity RAD, ISS about 0.20-0.36 mGy/day from OSDR EDA, both labelled detector dose).

- Offline version: one file of about 5 MB with all voice files and images, making no external requests. In an offline test, all 5 bundled datasets validated at start-up.

EVIDENCE

- 75/75 unit tests pass; TypeScript typecheck passes; lint shows 0 errors.

- Scripted browser play-through (end-to-end test) passes 45/45.

- No console errors during manual play.

- Playtest with children.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

TypeScript, React 19, three.js with @react-three/fiber and drei (3D world), Zustand (game state and saving), Tailwind CSS 4, Vite 8 with vite-plugin-singlefile (offline build), Vitest and oxlint (testing). Python with requests, pypdf, netCDF4 and numpy for the NASA data pipeline and verification scripts. No special hardware: a desktop or laptop with a modern browser.

BENEFITS AND GOALS

- Children learn by deciding, not only by reading.

- They see why life-support numbers matter: one choice changes how many sols the crew can last.

- They learn to tell a measurement from a model, a forecast and a game rule.

- Arabic-speaking children can play the whole game in their own language, and schools with weak internet can use the offline file.

KNOWN LIMITS (this is a prototype)

- Only Mission 01 is playable.

- Designed for desktop or laptop with keyboard and mouse.

- Outdoor temperatures come from the NASA Ames Mars climate model, not measurements at Gale Crater.

- Radiation values are detector dose, not body dose. The game calculates no health effects.

- DONKI solar events were measured near Earth, not at Mars; the game uses them as real examples of solar events and forecast timing.

- Noor's English voice is a placeholder made with Windows speech synthesis.

FUTURE PLANS

- Replace modelled temperatures with measured temperatures from Curiosity's REMS weather station.

- Mission 2, "The Long Storm".

- A silent robot exploration companion as a Mission 2 reward (it will not carry a second crate, because the one-crate limit is the core lesson).

- A lunar south-pole mission using Moon Trek illumination and Earth-visibility layers.

- A teacher guide.

- Touch play on tablets and phones.
